newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Violence deals another blow to Israeli tourism.
newsitem.headline: Violence deals another blow to Israeli tourism.

text.p: Israel's beleaguered tourism industry could suffer yet another blow from the outbreak of violence in the West Bank and Gaza, but industry officials hope this week's Washington summit may yet salvage the sector.

At an emergency meeting on Monday sponsored by the Tourism Ministry, industry officials estimated that losses from cancelled reservations in the wake of the clashes between Palestinians and Israelis could reach $200 million.

That would deal a heavy blow to an industry that had placed great hopes on Middle East peace as a spur to increased foreign tourism. This year alone it has been pummelled by a wave of suicide bombings in February and March, fighting between Israel and Hizbollah guerrillas based in Lebanon in April and the recent TWA jet crash in the United States.

The immediate impact of last week's clashes between Israeli soldiers and Palestinians has not been enormous, say industry officals. But there is a potential for a bigger fallout later on, if violence resumes.

David Fatal, managing director of Africa Israel Hotels, which has seven Holiday Inns in Israel, said he had seen relatively few cancellations in the last week. "But we are concerned about reservations for the winter season," he said.
The Tourism Ministry said there has been a halt in new flight and hotel reservations.

"People -- tour operators and groups -- are waiting to see the results of the (Washington summit) talks," said Nachman Klieman, spokesman for the Israeli national airline El Al. "If the results are good, cancellations will stop."
U.S. President Bill Clinton convened an Arab-Israeli summit in Washington to defuse tension between Israelis and Palestinians and get peace talks back on track.
The tourism industry, which last year had revenues of $3.3 billion, has also been hurt by purely economic factors, said Pnina Ben-David, an economist for the Israel Hotels Association.
Israel's strong currency, the shekel, cuts into the profits of hotels and other businesses that rely on overseas tourism.

Relatively high inflation, running at an annual rate of about 12 percent, raises operating costs. But the failure of the dollar to strengthen against the shekel in line with inflation over the last three years has meant that revenues do not keep pace.

El Al, which flew 2.93 million passengers in 1995, saw passenger loads drop sharply in the first nine months of the year. "What we're experiencing today is a decrease of 12 to 18 percent," Klieman said. The drop would have been more severe, except that Israelis are travelling more, he added.

Overnight stays in Israeli hotels by foreign tourists were down only two percent from January to August, compared with a year ago, to 6.2 million, according to the hotels association. But that was because of high occupancy levels in the first three months of the year. In the summer, overnight stays were down 14 to 22 percent from a year earlier, Ben-David said.
The hotels have been helped in part by domestic tourism, which was up nine percent in the first eight months.
